ideas.rationale: Most three-dimensional of the three: four distinct stone-shape families (straight/corner/tee/cross) each carrying trenches, tally notches, and 45-degree chamfers, plus a genuinely different font-stone part (basin + owner holes), a scoop draw bin, and four spur wells break the board's silhouette out of a plain slab. Part vocabulary and silhouette language ('mason's yard mid-project') read as a real object rather than hardware; must_survive conditions (bin opening, hole/notch counts) risk real geometry.

The capacity-gauge twist on Kalah is a real mechanical idea, but the object itself is thin: a plain trough of round wells plus one 0.5mm-deep engraved ring and three sizes of plain cylinder is most of the geometry on offer. 'An old measuring device set out on a table' is close to instrument-comparison territory even though it stops short of lab-jig language, and there is only one carved feature family carrying identity.

Declared as an exact reskin with no rule change, so the mechanical ambition is zero by design; the object compensates with a nice dual-relief disc (rings vs radial fan) but the board is a single repeated hollow-and-ridge grid with no part-family variety, so most of the piece count is one part type stamped 64 times rather than a built vocabulary.
